name: Asparagus
label: asparagus bed

planting.note: five crowns per person is the UMaine rule of thumb; a 4x8 bed holds two rows of seven 1-ft-apart crowns

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart in a 30 in bed; UMaine wants 5 ft between commercial rows, but a bed only works if you accept denser, shorter-lived planting

watch_for: asparagus beetle and spotted asparagus beetle chewing spear tips, Fusarium crown rot on wet low-pH soil, asparagus rust on damp ferns
watering: One inch a week for the first three years to build the bed; established plants need water only in serious drought (UMaine).
method_notes: The classic permanent bed — Coleman treats it as the anchor of the perennial corner, established once and then out of the rotation for 15-20 years (The New Organic Grower). Prepare soil to 10-12 in deep and lime to 6.5-7.0 pH a season before planting; a poor bed can't be fixed later. Plant one-year-old crowns (healthy roots are white inside, not reddish-brown) after soil warms past 50F. Year-one discipline is total: no harvest at all; year two harvest two weeks, year three three weeks, year four four, and stop by June 15 in Maine so ferns rebuild the crown. Male hybrids (Jersey Knight, Jersey Supreme, Jersey Giant) out-yield and outlive the old open-pollinated types. Do not plant where asparagus has grown before.
source: UMaine Bulletin #2071 Growing Asparagus in Maine; Eliot Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.), perennial crops chapter.

permanent.note: Needs a deep, well-drained, weed-free site prepared a year ahead; lime to 6.5-7.0 pH before planting. It is a permanent, once-planted bed occupying ground for 15-20 years, so it never rotates through the vegetable beds.

name: Rhubarb
label: rhubarb crowns

planting.note: two crowns fill a 4x8 bed; UMaine spacing is 3-4 ft each way, 5 ft for the big varieties

bed30.note: one crown every 3-4 ft; a single mature crown exceeds 4 ft across, so a whole 30 in bed holds one plant comfortably

watch_for: crown rot in wet heavy soil, leaf fungal spots in cool damp weather, rhubarb curculio in weedy plantings
watering: Drought tolerant once established; in hot dry spells soak to 3-6 in deep (roots feed at 12-18 in, so water hard, not often).
method_notes: A cool-climate crop that needs our cold winters to go dormant — no Maine chill problem at all. Best started as a divided crown with 1-2 eyes and at least a 2-in cross-section of storage root; seed gives variable plants. Do NOT harvest any stalks in year one; harvest from year two on, never more than half the stalks, and stop by about August 31 so the crown rebuilds for winter. Remove flower stalks as they form. Dig, split and replant the crown every four to five years to keep stalks thick. Leaves are oxalic-acid toxic; stalks only.
source: UMaine Bulletin #2514 Growing Rhubarb in Maine; Eliot Coleman, The New Organic Grower (3rd ed.), perennial crops chapter.

permanent.note: Well-drained loam, full sun, generous spacing (3-4 ft) — a crown rewards space and forgives most soils. It occupies its corner for a decade or more and gets split every 4-5 years, so it never rotates through the annual beds.

name: Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke)
label: sunchoke hedge

planting.note: plant pieces 4 in deep, 12-14 in apart along a row — feed the hedge at the back of the garden

bed30.note: one row, tubers 12-14 in apart; this is a tall hedge plant, not a bed occupant

watch_for: few pests; the persistence is the pest — missed tubers resprout, so plant where it can spread; white mold in wet years
watering: Soak at planting, then mostly none — established plants shrug off drought and produce in poor soil.
method_notes: Native sunflower relative, hardy as Maine gets. Plant tubers 3-4 in deep in early spring after frost; a pound of seed tubers makes an 18-20 ft row. It grows a 6-8 ft flowering hedge by fall — treat it as a productive screen, not a bed crop. Harvest after a couple of frosts sweetens the tubers; dig what you need, leave the rest in the ground (they store perfectly in situ) and re-plant a few small tubers each spring, or it will wander. Once in, it is nearly impossible to eradicate, so site it deliberately. Coleman lists it among the winter-harvestable perennials (Four-Season Harvest).
source: Fedco sunchoke growing notes and Johnny's Selected Seeds Jerusalem artichoke key growing information; Eliot Coleman, Four-Season Harvest, winter crops chapter.

permanent.note: Grows almost anywhere but prefers light sandy soil; full sun for best tuber bulk. It is a self-perpetuating, spreading perennial that never leaves the garden once planted — a deliberate permanent hedge, not a rotation crop.

name: Sea kale
label: sea kale crowns

planting.note: eight crowns at 18-24 in spacing fill a 4x8 bed of its own

bed30.note: one row, 18-24 in apart; plants form a 1-3 ft rosette with 3 ft flower racemes

watch_for: flea beetles on young growth (it is a brassica), slugs in wet springs; deer will graze the young leaves
watering: Water well through the first season; once established it is a tough coastal perennial that takes dry spells and salt wind.
method_notes: The old English asparagus-substitute: a zone-5 hardy perennial brassica from the seashore. Start from root cuttings taken in winter (easier and truer than seed), or scarified seed started indoors like broccoli. Let it settle in year one — harvest begins the second year and improves after. The Victorian trick Coleman describes in Four-Season Harvest is forcing: cover crowns with an opaque pot or bucket in early spring and the blanched, pale shoots are the delicacy — cut at 3-10 in before they green. Leave the plants to leaf out after forcing so they rebuild for next year. Best in sharp-draining, even slightly chalky soil; part shade is fine, unlike asparagus.
source: Fedco Sea Kale Perennial Greens listing (hardiness, culture, forcing); Royal Horticultural Society Crambe maritima plant page; Eliot Coleman, Four-Season Harvest.

permanent.note: A true perennial vegetable occupying permanent ground for a decade. Sharp-draining, sandy or chalky soil, full sun to part shade; thrives near coast. Never rotated — a permanent crown planting harvested for its forced spring shoots.

name: Strawberry
label: strawberry matted row

planting.note: ten plants per 4x8 matted row at 18 in spacing; 100 plants feeds a family of four with surplus

bed30.note: one matted row, plants 18 in apart, row held to 24 in wide with runners pinned back

watch_for: gray mold (Botrytis) in wet June weather, tarnished plant bug and strawberry bud weevil distorting fruit, red stele and Verticillium root rots — buy resistant varieties and move sites
watering: One to two inches a week through fruit set; soaker the rows, not overhead, to keep gray mold down.
method_notes: Technically perennial, practically a 3-5 year bed — plan to replant on fresh ground (never where tomatoes/peppers/eggplant grew: Verticillium). June-bearers: plant early spring, pinch ALL flowers the first year so runners fill an 18-in-apart matted row, mulch with 6-8 in of straw in mid-November and pull it off in spring. Earliglow, Wendy, Cavendish, Flavorfest and Jewel are the UMaine-tested performers. A fall/winter planting of day-neutrals (Seascape, Albion, Tribute, Tristar) can be grown as an annual for later fruit. Beds decline hard after year three — rotating through new ground is the honest plan.
source: UMaine Bulletin #2067 Growing Strawberries (site, spacing, varieties, renovation).

permanent.note: A short-lived perennial that must rotate: plant on new ground every 3-5 years to dodge soil-borne root rots. Full sun, sandy loam, 18-in matted rows. Not a permanent bed in the asparagus sense — it is a renewable perennial.

name: Blackberry
label: blackberry hills

planting.note: hill system: two plants per 4x8 at 4 ft apart, rows 8-12 ft

bed30.note: not a bed crop — hill system at 4 ft, rows 8-12 ft, trellised; canes grow 4-6 ft

watch_for: spotted wing drosophila on ripe fruit (pick daily, chill immediately), cane borers, viruses — plant certified virus-free stock and destroy wild brambles within 600 ft
watering: One to two inches a week in the season; drought during ripening makes hard, small berries.
method_notes: Hardiness is the honest catch: UMaine says blackberries lack the hardiness for anywhere but well-sheltered southern Maine sites — temps below 5F injure or kill the canes, so Wiscasset is the right edge of the map (coastal shelter helps). Plant dormant one-year canes in spring, hill system at 4 ft; trellis or they flop. Thorny Darrow and Illini are the varieties UMaine lists; thornless types need even milder sites. Fruit comes on second-year canes: pinch new canes at 4 ft to force fruiting laterals, then cut out every cane that fruited, right after harvest. Netting for birds, and pick daily in the SWD window.
source: UMaine Bulletin #2066 Growing Raspberries and Blackberries (hardiness limits, hill spacing, pruning); Bulletin #2172 Raspberry and Blackberry Varieties for Maine (Darrow, Illini).

permanent.note: Perennial roots, biennial canes — each cane fruits once then dies, so it lives as a managed hedgerow with a trellis, outside the rotation. Full sun, well-drained sandy loam. Marginal hardiness in zone 5b: plant only in a sheltered, south-facing site.

name: Highbush blueberry
label: highbush blueberry bushes

planting.note: one bush per 4x8 — this is an orchard/hedge plant at 5-7 ft spacing, not a bed crop

bed30.note: 5-7 ft between plants, 8-10 ft between rows; netted against birds when fruit colors

watch_for: blueberry maggot in ripe fruit, mummy berry shriveling berries in wet springs, birds (netting is the only effective control)
watering: One to two inches a week; shallow roots — a 4-6 in mulch layer of pine needles or wood chips is the best watering tool.
method_notes: Soil is everything: highbush blueberry needs pH 4.5-5.2 and won't wait while you amend later — test and acidify with sulfur well before planting. Plant 2-3 year nursery bushes in early spring at 5-7 ft; two or more varieties improve set and spread the season (Patriot, Northland, Bluecrop, Blueray are UMaine's northern picks). Year-one and -two discipline: pick off all flower clusters both years, tolerate a small crop in year three, full crop at four to five. Prune dormant, January-March: canes older than six years come out. Protect below -25F is the real zone limit — Wiscasset coastal is fine.
source: UMaine Bulletin #2253 Growing Highbush Blueberries (pH, spacing, varieties, pruning, pests).

permanent.note: Demands acid, well-drained sandy loam rich in organic matter — a dedicated ericaceous bed, kept separate from lime-loving vegetables. A 20-30 year permanent shrub planting, renewed by cane pruning, never rotated.

name: Lowbush blueberry (wild blueberry)
label: wild blueberry patch

planting.note: 1 ft x 1 ft sod blocks, set 1-2 ft apart; one block per 4x8, or sod a dedicated patch

bed30.note: two rows, plants/sod 1-2 ft apart; they spread into a ground-cover patch

watch_for: blueberry maggot and mummy berry (same as highbush), woody weed competition — cut saplings and ferns three times a year; birds at ripeness
watering: About one inch a week, spread over the week, for the first two establishment years and in dry crop years; extra water invites disease.
method_notes: Maine's native crop — the state's blueberry program is built on it. Wild blueberries want acidic pH 4.0-4.5, sandy well-drained soil, and full sun; they will NOT grow in a vegetable bed, so give them their own patch. Easiest route is transplanting sod (1 ft blocks) from a reputable nursery, or buy plants 1-2 ft apart. Pinch off ALL blossoms the first two years so roots establish — the single most important discipline. Then manage on a two-year mow cycle: mow half the patch to 1.5 in every fall, alternate sides yearly, and you get berries every year. About half a pound per square foot once established (year four).
source: UMaine Bulletin #2073 Growing Wild Blueberries at Home (soil, pH, sod, mowing cycle, water); UMaine Home Garden Lowbush Blueberry Planting Guide.

permanent.note: Native to Maine's acid, sandy, well-drained coastal soils — replicate those conditions or it fails. A permanent ground-cover patch (1-2 ft tall) managed on a biennial mowing cycle, entirely outside the vegetable rotation.

name: Red currant
label: red currant bushes

planting.note: two bushes per 4x8 at 3-5 ft spacing; rows 8-10 ft

bed30.note: one row, plants 3-5 ft apart — currants tolerate more shade than most fruit

watch_for: currant aphids curling new leaves, powdery mildew, anthracnose leaf spot in wet years, currant borer tunneling canes; white pine blister rust is the regulatory pest
watering: Keep the root zone cool and moist — 2-3 in of mulch does most of the work; this is not a drought-tolerant bush.
method_notes: IMPORTANT — LEGAL FIRST: Maine quarantines all Ribes (currants and gooseberries) to protect white pine from blister rust, and Wiscasset is in Lincoln County, one of the fully prohibited counties on the Maine Forest Service quarantine list. Sale, transport, further planting and possession are prohibited. If any pine is nearby, plant something else. Where legal (check your county): currants are the easiest berries in the Northeast, fruiting in June on 2-3 year wood. Plant 1-2 year stock in early fall or very early spring, remove all first-year flowers, expect a light crop year two and full crop year three. Prune dormant, keeping about 6-8 bearing canes by renewal — older wood fruits poorly. Rovada is a reliable red; they prefer pH about 6.5 and tolerate part shade.
source: Cornell Fruit Resources: Gooseberries and Currants (site, spacing, pruning, pests); Maine Forest Service white pine blister rust quarantine via UMaine Extension Ask the Expert 2024.

permanent.note: Cool, moist, well-drained soil with organic matter; tolerates partial shade. A permanent shrub maintained by cane renewal pruning. LEGAL CHECK REQUIRED: Ribes are under quarantine in Lincoln County, Maine (white pine blister rust) — do not plant without confirming current county status.

name: Black currant
label: black currant bushes

planting.note: two bushes per 4x8 at 3-5 ft spacing; rows 8-10 ft

bed30.note: one row, plants 3-5 ft apart

watch_for: currant aphids, powdery mildew, leaf spot; black currants are the most susceptible Ribes to white pine blister rust — the quarantine pest
watering: Keep the root zone cool and moist with mulch; consistent water through fruit swell in early summer.
method_notes: Same Maine legal warning as red currant — Ribes quarantine covers black currants in Lincoln County (Wiscasset); check the Maine Forest Service map before planning anything. Note the historical federal ban targeted black currants specifically as the most rust-susceptible. Where legal, the resistant cultivars (Consort, Crusader, Titania — bred immune or resistant to blister rust) are the only sensible choice in the Northeast. Culture mirrors red currant: 3-5 ft spacing, remove first-year flowers, full crop by year three, dormant renewal pruning of canes older than three years. Fruit is much higher in vitamin C than red currants and makes the classic currant jelly.
source: Cornell Fruit Resources: Gooseberries and Currants (cultivars, culture, pruning); UMaine Extension Ask the Expert on the Maine Ribes quarantine.

permanent.note: Cool, moist, well-drained soil, part shade OK. Use only blister-rust resistant cultivars where legal. LEGAL CHECK REQUIRED: black currants are the most rust-susceptible Ribes and are under quarantine in Lincoln County, Maine.

name: Gooseberry
label: gooseberry bushes

planting.note: two bushes per 4x8 at 3-5 ft spacing; rows 8-10 ft

bed30.note: one row, plants 3-5 ft apart; goosberries can be trellised to add airflow and ease picking

watch_for: powdery mildew (the big one on European types — pick American cultivars), currant aphids, gooseberry fruitworm webbing berries, San Jose scale on old wood
watering: Mulch and keep cool and moist; gooseberries suffer in hot dry sites, so a north-side or lightly shaded spot beats full sun here.
method_notes: Legal warning identical to the currants — gooseberries are Ribes and fall under the same Maine quarantine covering Lincoln County (Wiscasset); verify county status before planting. Where legal, the American types (Poorman, Oregon Champion, Pixwell, Hinnonmaki Red/Yellow, Captivator) are the healthier, mildew-resistant choice in the East — European cultivars have the big fruit and the worst mildew. Culture like currants: remove first-year flowers, light crop year two, full by year three. Fruiting is on 2-3 year wood, so use the renewal-pruning pattern (about 8 bearing canes). Trellising the bushes improves air flow and harvest. Berries ripen over two weeks in late June; pick when colored.
source: Cornell Fruit Resources: Gooseberries and Currants (American vs European types, spacing, mildew, pruning); UMaine Extension on the Maine Ribes quarantine.

permanent.note: Cool, moist, well-drained soil; prefers light shade in the Northeast, which makes it genuinely different from the full-sun berries. Permanent shrub maintained by renewal pruning. LEGAL CHECK REQUIRED: under Ribes quarantine in Lincoln County, Maine.

name: Elderberry
label: elderberry hedgerow

planting.note: one plant per 4x8 — this is a hedgerow shrub at 6-10 ft spacing, not a bed crop

bed30.note: shrubs 6-10 ft apart; they sucker into a hedgerow and shade everything within reach

watch_for: powdery mildew in humid spells, cane borers in old canes, birds on the clusters; virtually pest-free otherwise
watering: Keep well watered the entire first season — roots are shallow and the plants dry out fast; then only in real drought.
method_notes: The most reliable 'native orchard' berry in Maine: hardy to zone 3, flowers late June so spring frosts almost never hit it. Nearly self-unfruitful, so plant two different cultivars within 60 ft (Adams 1 & 2, York, Johns, Nova are proven; UMaine runs elderberry workshops exactly because it thrives here). Shallow-rooted — never cultivate deeper than 2 in, hand-pull weeds, mulch. Canes fruit on the current season's growth, especially on second-year laterals, so the pruning rule is simple: in late winter remove all canes older than three years and keep one-, two- and three-year canes in balance. Harvest whole clusters late August-early September; uncooked berries are astringent and inedible. Cook before use. Grows in far wetter ground than most fruit, but not standing water.
source: Cornell Cooperative Extension, Elderberries (gardening.cals.cornell.edu fruit factsheet): culture, spacing, pruning, harvest; UMaine Extension small-fruit programming.

permanent.note: Moist, fertile, well-drained soil, pH 5.5-6.5, full sun to part shade; tolerant of wetter ground than most berries. A suckering hedgerow shrub that must have room — not a bed crop. Renewed by cutting out canes older than three years.

name: Honeyberry (haskap)
label: honeyberry row

planting.note: two bushes per 4x8 at 3-4 ft in-row; rows 6-10 ft

bed30.note: one row, plants 3-4 ft apart; bushes reach 4-6 ft tall and wide

watch_for: birds (net late May-early June — they find it first, it is the earliest fruit here), powdery mildew on susceptible cultivars, sunscald on exposed fruit
watering: Not drought tolerant — moist, never soggy; drip is ideal. Deep water every 5-7 days in the high-summer stretch.
method_notes: A genuinely cold-climate berry (native down to zone 2 plains and Scandinavian/Alaskan coasts) that thrives in Maine winters but needs two cultivars that bloom together for cross-pollination — most nurseries sell compatible pairs. Extremely early: ripens early to mid June, before strawberries, and the flowers take frost to about 19F, so springs here rarely cost the crop. Site in full sun with well-drained soil; pH is broadly adaptable. Light harvest begins year 3-4, mature bushes give 5-15 lb. Tundra, Borealis, Indigo Gem and Blue Lightning are the well-documented cultivars. Prune lightly in late winter — no more than a quarter of the bush — thinning oldest branches for air.
source: Utah State University Extension, Haskap in the Garden (peer-reviewed; culture, spacing, cultivars, frost tolerance); Fedco/Johnny's haskap listings for New England availability.

permanent.note: Long-lived shrub (to 30 years), broadly pH-adaptable, needs moist well-drained soil and a second cultivar for pollination. Earliest-ripening berry in a Maine garden — a permanent planting that no annual bed can substitute for.

name: Apple
label: apple trees

planting.note: not a bed crop — dwarf trees at 6-8 ft spacing, semi-dwarf at 15 ft in cold regions

bed30.note: semi-dwarf 15 ft, dwarf 6-8 ft, standard 25 ft; cold-region spacing per UMaine

watch_for: apple scab in our wet springs (plant resistant varieties), cedar-apple rust where junipers grow nearby, apple maggot and codling moth in the fruit, deer and voles on young trees
watering: Five gallons a week per young tree in any week with under an inch of rain, through the first few growing seasons.
method_notes: The most winter-hardy tree fruit and the one Maine does best — most varieties are at home here; the coastal 5b/6a site is prime apple country. Plant bare-root in April/early May (fall planting is wrong for New England), graft union 2-3 in above ground, stake dwarf trees, never fertilize the planting hole. Train to central leader, head whips to 30-36 in. Most varieties need a second, compatible variety for pollination — plant two that bloom together. Scab is the disease that decides everything in a wet climate: choose resistant varieties (Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom, Pristine, CrimsonCrisp per UMaine) or spray from green tip. Dwarf on M.9/M.26 yields in year 3-4; be honest that standard trees take 6-8. Pick a mix that ripens from August into October.
source: UMaine Cooperative Extension, Growing Fruit Trees in Maine: Types of Fruit Trees, Spacing Trees in an Orchard, Bulletin #2411 Planting and Early Care of Fruit Trees.

permanent.note: Full sun, well-drained soil, at least 6 hours direct light; semi-dwarf at 15 ft spacing, dwarf at 6-8 ft. A permanent orchard tree producing for decades — entirely outside the vegetable rotation, with pollination, scab and deer management built in for the life of the tree.

name: Pear (European)
label: pear trees

planting.note: not a bed crop — pears are the largest tree fruit, give them the extra 5 ft beyond apple spacing

bed30.note: semi-dwarf pears about 20 ft, standards 30 ft — pears need an additional 5 ft over apples (UMaine)

watch_for: fire blight (the defining pear disease in the East — plant resistant varieties), pear psylla, codling moth; deer browse young trees
watering: Same as apple: five gallons a week while young whenever rain is under an inch; mature trees mostly fend for themselves.
method_notes: Pears are hardier than their reputation — the cold-hardy European varieties are rated for zone 4 and do fine in coastal Maine. The honest catches: they are the slowest of the tree fruits to bear (commonly 5-7 years even on dwarfing stock — plan for it), and fire blight decides the variety list: plant resistant types (Harrow Delight, Magness, Maxine, Potomac, Seckel per UMaine; Blake's Pride for market quality). They also grow large: give them the extra 5 ft beyond apple spacing. Two compatible varieties needed for pollination. Central-leader training, keep the crotch angles wide (45-60 deg) — narrow crotches split with a heavy crop. Asian pears are zone 5 but dislike Maine's winter temperature swings, so European types are the honest recommendation for Wiscasset.
source: UMaine Cooperative Extension, Types of Fruit Trees (pear varieties and hardiness), Spacing Trees in an Orchard.

permanent.note: Full sun, well-drained soil; the largest of the hardy tree fruits, needing generous spacing (20 ft semi-dwarf, 30 ft standard). Slow to come into bearing (5-7 years) but very long-lived. Permanent orchard tree outside the rotation.

name: Plum (hybrid/European)
label: plum trees

planting.note: not a bed crop — one tree per 4x8 plus orchard space; 10-18 ft between trees by rootstock

bed30.note: Myrobalan rootstock: 15-18 ft vigorous varieties, 12-15 ft low vigor (UMaine)

watch_for: black knot on branches (the plum disease — prune out galls), plum curculio scarring fruit, rain splitting on Shiro/Methley/Superior, frost on the early bloom (plums flower a week before apples)
companions: another plum of the same type
watering: Water young trees weekly in dry spells (2-5 gal); mature trees want no wet feet — well-drained site decides success.
method_notes: Plums do well in Maine, with one calendar warning: they bloom about a week before apples, so a late frost can take the crop — plant on a slope with good air drainage, not in a frost pocket. Two pollination rules that matter: Japanese plums must be planted with other Japanese-type varieties (they will not pollinate from Europeans and vice versa), and Europeans (Stanley, Italian) are the hardier, more reliable choice for zone 5b. UMaine's hardy standouts include Toka, Superior, Alderman, Black Ice, LaCrescent. Trees begin bearing the third year and hit full production about year eight. Black knot is the disease to watch — remove infected branches in late winter and pick knot-resistant varieties (Toka, Obilinaja, Superior). Most rootstocks sucker heavily; keep the base clean.
source: UMaine Bulletin #2034 Plum Production in Maine (varieties, rootstocks, spacing, pollination, black knot); Types of Fruit Trees for hardiness zones.

permanent.note: Full sun on a slope with air drainage — plums bloom early and the site is half the crop protection. Well-drained soil, pH 6.0-7.0, 12-18 ft spacing by rootstock. Permanent orchard tree; Japanese and European types must each be matched with their own kind for pollination.

name: Sweet cherry
label: sweet cherry tree

planting.note: not a bed crop — dwarf sweet cherries today, at 6-8 ft; standard trees are huge and difficult to net

bed30.note: dwarf sweet cherry 6-8 ft (spacing page); non-dwarf types get extra 5 ft beyond apples

watch_for: spring frost on the earliest bloom of any fruit tree, brown rot on ripening fruit, cherry fruit fly maggots, birds — netting is mandatory or the tree is a bird feeder
watering: Five gallons a week while establishing; keep soil even at fruit swell to reduce cracking.
method_notes: HONESTY FIRST: sweet cherry is marginal in zone 5b. UMaine's zone guidance puts sweet cherries among the fruits that 'suffer winter injury in colder years' even in zone 5, and its cherry recommendations for a mild coastal 5b site steer to tart and duke cherries instead — the sweet cherry's early bloom is a standing invitation to frost, and it is the most disease-susceptible of the cherries. If you try one anyway in Wiscasset's coastal moderation: choose a self-fertile, late-blooming variety (Lapins, Stella, Sweetheart), on dwarfing rootstock so you can actually net it, on the warmest slope you have. Expect a crop roughly every other year. Otherwise, a tart or duke cherry is the honest, productive choice.
source: UMaine Cooperative Extension: Types of Fruit Trees (hardiness zones, disease susceptibility); Ask the Expert: hardy sweet or tart cherry recommendations for a zone 5b Maine site.

permanent.note: MARGINAL in zone 5b: sweet cherries bloom earliest, suffer winter injury in cold years and need dwarf rootstock plus netting. Full sun, well-drained slope, 6-8 ft for dwarfs. Treat as an experiment here; a tart or duke cherry is the reliably productive choice.

name: Tart (sour) cherry
label: tart cherry tree

planting.note: not a bed crop — one tree; naturally a semidwarf tree at 15 ft spacing

bed30.note: semidwarf at about 15 ft, like a semidwarf apple

watch_for: brown rot in wet weather as fruit ripens, cherry fruit fly maggots, birds (net); far less bothered by frost and disease than sweet cherry
watering: Five gallons a week while establishing; even moisture at fruit swell to prevent cracking.
method_notes: This is the honest cherry for zone 5b: naturally semidwarf (12-18 ft), genuinely winter hardy, self-fruitful, and tolerant of spring freezes that would destroy a sweet cherry crop. UMaine's coastal-Maine cherry recommendations are tart varieties — Carmine Jewel, Evans, Mesabi, Meteor, North Star — plus the duke hybrids (Balaton, May Duke, Almaden) which carry sweet-cherry flavor with sour-cherry hardiness. Plant in early spring, graft union above ground, open-center training for stone fruits. It blooms with or slightly after apples, still early, so give it a slope with air drainage. Fruit ripens late June-early July; pick before birds do and net if you want a full harvest. Trees begin to bear by year 3-4.
source: UMaine Cooperative Extension: Ask the Expert cherry recommendations for zone 5b Maine (June 2022); Types of Fruit Trees (sour cherry hardiness and form).

permanent.note: Full sun, well-drained soil, air-drained slope. The hardy, productive cherry for zone 5b — a naturally semidwarf permanent tree, self-fruitful, renewed by annual dormant pruning. Outside the vegetable rotation.

name: Peach
label: peach tree

planting.note: not a bed crop — one tree at 15 ft, or 8 ft with annual pruning

bed30.note: 15 ft traditional spacing; 8 ft possible with annual pruning in Maine's cold-limited growth (UMaine)

watch_for: peach leaf curl (the defining disease — Redhaven has good resistance, Reliance poor), brown rot on ripening fruit, peach tree borer at the trunk base, plum curculio; winter kills flower buds below about -10F
watering: 2-5 gallons per tree during dry spells; mulch 3-4 in with wood chips, keeping it off the trunk (nothing that invites voles).
method_notes: The honest truth from UMaine's peach specialist: peach trees in Maine live about seven years on average — severely cold winters can kill them at any age — and bloom mid-May, usually (but not always) escaping frost. This is a 'gamble that pays deliciously' crop in zone 5b, not a reliable one. If you plant: hardiest varieties only — Contender, Reliance, Redhaven, Cresthaven all have good flower-bud hardiness and were evaluated by UMaine at Highmoor Farm in zone 5b; Glowingstar and the donut peach BuenOsII are newer good-bud-hardiness picks. Site on a slope with air drainage, full sun, pH 6.0-7.0. Expect fewer fruit whenever winter dips below -10F; prune late (April, after cold passes) to preserve flower buds; thin fruit hard. Harvest late July through late September by spot-picking.
source: UMaine Bulletin #2068 Growing Peaches in Maine (life expectancy, hardy varieties, site, pruning, harvest); Types of Fruit Trees (zone adaptability).

permanent.note: MARGINAL in zone 5b: UMaine puts lifetime expectancy at roughly 7 years in Maine, with winter bud kill below -10F the usual end. Needs full sun on an air-drained slope, pH 6.0-7.0. Plant the hardiest varieties and treat as a short-lived delight, not a long-term tree.

name: Quince
label: quince tree

planting.note: not a bed crop — one tree; naturally dwarf so it needs less space than most fruit trees

bed30.note: naturally dwarf tree, about 10 ft spacing

watch_for: fire blight and quince rust (most varieties lack resistance — the honest risk), codling moth; flower buds damaged in severe winters
watering: Regular water through establishment and fruit swell; mature trees tolerate dry spells.
method_notes: Quince is a niche fruit with real limits in zone 5b. Per UMaine: most quince are hardy to zone 5 (-20F) and a few to zone 4, so Wiscasset sits at the edge of its range; fruit needs a LONG growing season, so on the coast (which buys us weeks of fall warmth) choose a short-season variety — Smyrna, Van Deman, Limon and Pineapple are the named ones. The honest warnings: nearly all varieties lack resistance to fire blight and quince rust (two diseases Maine's damp June weather encourages), and the fruit is rock-hard and astringent until cooked — it is strictly a jelly/preserve fruit. It is naturally dwarf, self-fruitful, and beautiful in flower, which is most people's real reason to grow it. Treat as a southern-Maine specialty, site warm, and don't count on it the way you'd count on an apple.
source: UMaine Cooperative Extension, Types of Fruit Trees (quince hardiness, varieties, diseases); Fedco Trees availability for the named varieties.

permanent.note: MARGINAL but viable in zone 5b coastal sites. Naturally dwarf tree needing less room; hardy to roughly -20F. Needs a long, warm fall to ripen fruit and has weak disease resistance (fire blight, quince rust). A specimen/preserve fruit tree, not a production staple.

name: Hazelnut (American filbert)
label: hazelnut shrubs

planting.note: not a bed crop — one shrub per 4x8 at 10-15 ft spacing; plant more than one for nut set

bed30.note: 10-15 ft apart; a multi-stemmed shrub 12-18 ft tall and 10-15 ft wide

watch_for: eastern filbert blight (the disease that kills European hazels — American hazelnut is resistant), nut weevil leaving 'hit' marks on shells, squirrels/deer/voles/small rodents in the harvest
watering: Weekly water the first year until roots establish; after that, only in prolonged drought.
method_notes: The easiest nut for Maine: the native American hazelnut (Corylus americana) is blight-resistant, cold hardy to zone 4, pH-adaptable, and unfussy about soil — UMaine's own Master Gardener article calls it the perfect low-maintenance native nut. It grows as a multi-stemmed shrub (or pruned to a small tree), so it belongs in a hedgerow, not a bed. Needs cross-pollination — plant at least two (Fedco: plant more than one, 4-6 ft apart for a thicket, or 10-15 ft for specimen shrubs), wind carries the pollen. First nuts 3-5 years after planting, then dependable 40-50 year yields — about the third week of September in central Maine, when husks turn brown. Protection for the first three years is the weak point: cage against deer and voles or they'll eat the young ones. Hybrids (Jefferson, zone 5) give bigger European-type nuts with EFB resistance.
source: UMaine Home Garden News March 2022: American Hazelnut feature (hardiness, size, yields, harvest date, pests); Fedco Trees: American Hazelnut and Jefferson Hazelnut listings (spacing, culture).

permanent.note: American hazelnut: hardy zone 4, prefers well-drained soil but genuinely pH-adaptable, full sun for best nut set (light shade reduces yield). A multi-stemmed shrub 12-18 ft tall producing for 40-50 years. Needs a second plant for pollination; young plants must be caged from deer and voles for three years.
